newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief promises reform but not at any price.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief promises reform but not at any price.

text.p: Pledging to work for far-reaching changes in the United Nations, Secretary-General Kofi Annan said reform did not mean deep staff cuts.
In an address to employees, Annan, in office since Jan. 1, said managers would have more power to carry out policies and more responsibily for performance.
But he said that "sometimes it must seem that the United Nations does nothing but reform."

"I do not believe the disjointed incrementalism of the past, with its baggage of duplications and overlaps, was a positive evolution," he told cheering staff members gathered in the General Assembly hall on Thursday.
"Equally, I have never believed that disjointed downsizing, with arbitrary staff cuts that weaken essential capabilities, can bring real improvement," he said.
He has said he would come up with a plan for restructuring the United Nations that member states would have to approve, particularly in areas not directly under his control.
But his approach differs from that of Washington and conservatives in the U.S. Congress, who speak of reform primarily in terms of staff cuts.
The Clinton administration blocked a second five-year term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, alleging he did not move quickly enough on reform.

Annan, the first secretary-general chosen from within the U.N. bureaucracy, has instituted new procedures so that information could flow horizontally between department heads, an apparent indication that as the former head of peacekeeping he was sometimes unaware of issues that concerned him.
He has also attempted to encourage officials to deal more quickly with staff members charged with misconduct.
On Thursday, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard pointed to action on two potential scandals publicised in the media.
-- One was to dismiss Cheickh Mohamed Tidyane Bangoura of Guinea before his contract expired at the end of this month as an official of the U.N. drug control programme in Africa.

Although a decision had been made last summer not to renew his contract, Eckhard said Annan had spoken to the head of the Vienna-based programme, Giorgio Giacomelli, to release Bangoura earlier. Bangoura, now in Kenya, has been accused of nepotism and financial irregularities while he was based in the Ivory Coast. He has denied the charges.
-- The second case was to send a new acting chief of personnel to the Rwanda war crimes tribunal, based in Arusha, Tanzania.
The tribunal has been plagued by administrative difficulties and charges of nepotism.
Annan, a 58-year old Ghanian, in his speech also criticised the financial state of the United Nations, caused mainly because of Washington's arrears of about $1.3 billion.
"It is not reform when, for lack of funds we have to turn our backs on massacres and suffering and collapse of civil society," he said.

Annan intends to go to Washington on Jan. 23 at the invitation of President Bill Clinton. He is expected to visit Congress, the International Monetary Fund and address the National Press Club. He has been invited by Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, to meet commitee members over coffee.
